transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Yeah, um, nice to meet you. So, I guess... what finally made me come in today, after sort of going back and forth on whether I actually needed to see somebody, is that I've been having this really frustrating issue lately. 

I just finished my bachelor's, so right now I don't have a full-time job, and I've been spending a lot of time filling out applications and doing some independent research just to build up my portfolio and get my life started. But I keep turning in these applications, or submitting my research notes, with these small but just... incredibly embarrassing mistakes. 

And I mean, it's not like I'm just throwing them together and hitting send without looking. I'll sit there and go over the document, and I will honestly think I have checked everything perfectly. I'll feel totally confident about it. But then later I'll realize I completely mislabeled an artwork date in my notes, or I somehow just skipped an entire question on a job form. I look right at the page and my brain just doesn't see the blank space or the wrong number, I guess? And it's just making me look so careless and unprofessional to the people reading these things, even though I'm trying so hard to get it right. It's been driving me crazy, so I just... I figured I really needed to talk to a professional about why this keeps happening to me.

Beyond these mistakes with your applications, do you find that you spend a significant amount of your day feeling anxious or worried about many different areas of your life, such as your health, finances, or future, to the point where it is difficult to control these thoughts?

Um, no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, I guess it's a fair question, but I'm not really an anxious person in general? Like, when you mention health, I'm totally fine there. I try to stay somewhat active, maybe go for a run or hit the gym a couple of times a week—though honestly I've been slacking a little bit right after graduation just because the transition has been kind of weird—but I'm definitely not sitting around worrying that I'm sick or anything like that. 

And as for finances or the future... I mean, obviously I want a job, which is exactly why I'm doing all these applications in the first place. It would definitely be nice to have a steady paycheck and not have to stretch out the savings I made working at the campus library back in school. Which was a pretty great job, actually, mostly just organizing returns and helping people find reference books, but it didn't pay amazing. But even with the job hunt, I'm not, like, lying awake at night in a cold sweat panicking about going broke or my whole life falling apart. I know I'm only 21 and everyone takes a minute to get on their feet after their bachelor's. 

So it's really not this deep, uncontrollable dread about my life. It's really just the frustration with these specific mistakes. If I could just get my eyes to actually see the typo on the page, or notice that I skipped a box on a form before I hit submit, I'd feel completely fine. It's just that I keep doing it, and it makes me so mad at myself because I know I'm smart enough to fill out a basic form, you know? So, yeah, no spiraling thoughts about the future or anything. Just really, really annoyed about this one specific thing.

Do you find that you have these same types of issues with missing details or making careless mistakes when you are doing things other than job applications, such as in social situations, household chores, or during your leisure activities?

Well, um... I guess if I really think about it, I'm not totally sure? I mean, mostly it's the applications and the research notes that are really bothering me because those actually matter right now, you know? Like, if I mess up a cover letter, someone might just toss my resume in the trash, which is a big deal. 

But with other stuff... I don't know, it's hard to say. Like with chores, I live in an apartment with a couple of guys from college, and we sort of split things up. Mostly I just handle my own stuff, like my laundry or whatever. Sometimes I might leave a dish in the sink or forget to take the trash out right away, but I don't think I'm making, like, major careless mistakes with it? Or at least, if I am, it's not something my roommates are yelling at me about. We're all pretty laid back. I did accidentally shrink a couple of my favorite t-shirts last month because I just threw everything in the dryer on high heat without really checking the tags, which was super annoying, but I feel like everyone does that at some point, right?

And with hobbies or whatever, I spend a lot of time reading or just hanging out, playing some video games. I guess sometimes in games I might miss a small detail, like an item I was supposed to pick up, or I won't read the full quest description and then I end up wandering around for twenty minutes trying to figure out what I'm supposed to do. But again, it's a game, so it doesn't really feel like a "careless mistake" that ruins anything, it's just kind of how I play. 

Socially, I think I'm pretty normal. I don't think I'm missing details there. I mean, maybe I'll forget a birthday until I see it on social media, or I'll zone out for a second if a story is dragging on, but nothing crazy. So, honestly, I haven't really noticed it being a huge problem outside of the job hunt stuff. The applications are just where it's so incredibly obvious and frustrating, because the stakes are actually real, you know?

Looking back at your time in school or even now, do you often find it difficult to stay focused on tasks that you find boring or repetitive, to the point where you frequently lose track of time or forget what you were doing?

Well, um... I don't really think so? I mean, I guess it depends on what you mean by "difficult to stay focused," because honestly, if something is boring, isn't it hard for anyone to pay attention to it? Like, back in school, especially during my first couple of years when I was taking all those general education requirements—like this one geology class I had to take, which I thought was going to be about volcanoes and earthquakes and cool stuff like that, but it ended up just being memorizing different types of rocks and soil compositions for an entire semester. The professor was this older guy who just stood at the podium and read straight off his slides in this completely monotone voice. The slides were just walls of text, too, not even pictures of the rocks. It was brutal. I mean, in a class like that, yeah, my mind would wander. I'd start thinking about what I was going to have for lunch, or what I needed to do for my art history paper, or I'd just sort of doodle in the margins of my notebook. I used to draw these really elaborate little geometric patterns all down the side of the page just to keep myself awake. 

But I wouldn't say I was, like, completely losing track of time or forgetting what I was doing. I still knew I was in a geology lecture, you know? And I still managed to pass the class, even if I had to cram the night before the final because I hadn't absorbed much during the actual lectures. And with repetitive stuff now, like filling out the basic info sections on these job applications—name, address, education history, over and over and over again—it's definitely tedious. It feels like my brain just wants to shut down because it's so mind-numbingly dull to type the exact same dates of attendance for my bachelor's degree into fifty different online portals that all use slightly different formatting. 

But I don't just completely forget that I'm filling out an application. I might take a break, open a new tab, check Reddit or read an article about some new video game release just to give my brain a rest for five minutes, and maybe sometimes that five minutes turns into twenty minutes because I go down a rabbit hole reading about the game's development cycle or whatever. But I always come back to it. I know I have to finish it. So, yeah, boring stuff is boring, and I definitely don't love doing it, and I might get a little distracted, but I don't feel like I'm losing hours of my life or completely blanking on what my actual task is. It just feels like a normal reaction to doing something really tedious, you know? Like, nobody actually enjoys doing data entry for themselves all day.

When you are in situations where you are expected to stay seated for a long time, like in a movie theater, a long meeting, or even while working on your applications, do you often feel a strong urge to get up, fidget, or move around?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I have any issues with sitting still. Like, you mentioned a movie theater—I actually just went to see that new three-hour sci-fi epic with my roommates a couple of weeks ago. We went to the theater downtown, the one that recently upgraded to those really nice leather reclining seats, which are amazing by the way. But anyway, I sat there for the entire three hours and didn't get up once. Not even to use the restroom, which is honestly kind of a miracle because I had bought one of those massive bucket-sized sodas before the previews even started. But I was totally fine just sinking into the chair and watching the screen. I didn't feel restless or antsy at all.

And it's the same thing when I'm working on my applications. I can sit at my desk in my room for hours at a time. My desk chair isn't even that comfortable, honestly—it's this cheap, squeaky mesh thing I bought for like twenty bucks off a senior who was moving out of his dorm last year—but I don't feel like I'm crawling out of my skin needing to stand up or walk around. I mean, sure, I might shift my weight if my lower back starts to ache, or maybe I'll spin a pen around my fingers if I'm staring at my monitor trying to figure out how to word a cover letter, but I don't have this intense, driving urge to pace the room or anything like that. 

Actually, one of my roommates is exactly the way you're describing. Like, if we're just hanging out in the living room watching a thirty-minute sitcom, he's constantly bouncing his leg, or he gets up three different times to look inside the fridge even though we haven't bought groceries in a week, or he'll just start tossing a tennis ball against the wall. It drives me a little crazy sometimes, just watching him move non-stop. But for me? No, I'm pretty content just staying put. Once I'm seated, I'm kind of anchored there, especially if I have my laptop set up perfectly with my coffee on one side and my notebook on the other. So yeah, it's definitely more of a mental block with the boring stuff rather than a physical need to move around. I don't really get fidgety like that.
Looking back at your time in elementary school, did you frequently receive feedback from your teachers about being careless with your work or missing details on your assignments?

Oh, wow, going all the way back to elementary school... um, yeah. Actually, yes, definitely. It's funny you ask that because my mom is one of those people who saves absolutely everything, so she has this massive plastic storage bin in her attic with all my old report cards and parent-teacher conference notes. And if you look through them, there's definitely a very specific theme. 

Like, I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was super nice, always wore these really bright, hand-knit cardigans—she and pretty much all my other teachers would always write the exact same thing. They'd say that I was really engaged in class, you know, that I had really good ideas and contributed a lot when we were just talking about a book or doing a science experiment. But then, when it came to the actual assignments, it was a completely different story. 

I was always missing these little details on the assignments, or I would completely lose the instructions before I even made it home from the bus stop. I had this blue plastic take-home folder that was supposed to keep me organized, but it was just an absolute disaster zone of crumpled papers and broken pencils. And I think the most frustrating part for my teachers was that half the time, I would actually do the worksheet! Like, I'd sit at the kitchen table, finish the math problems, and shove it in my bag, but then the next day, I'd just completely forget to turn it in. It would just sit at the bottom of my backpack under my lunchbox for weeks. 

It actually got to the point where my parents had to step in and set up this strict nightly routine. Every single night, without fail, my mom or dad would make me dump my entire backpack out onto the living room rug, and they would physically check every single piece of paper to see what was in there. If they didn't check my backpack every night like that, I would just lose my worksheets or completely miss the details of what I was supposed to be bringing back to class. So, yeah, my teachers definitely gave that feedback a lot—it was always "great ideas, but he just can't keep track of his papers."

opening_question.question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a long-standing, persistent pattern of inattentiveness, characterized by careless mistakes and difficulties with organization, which has been present since elementary school and causes functional impairment in his current job application process.
